# Conservation of nose-touch avoidance across *C. elegans* and relatives

Nose touch avoidance behavior is conserved in five of the six species tested (Figure 5A). In *C. tripartitum*, animals showed an overall avoidance rate of less than 10% after the first few positive trials, which suggests this species adapts to the nose-touch stimulus faster than *C. elegans* and the others (Figure 5A). In the first three trials, however, *C. tripartitum* responded at levels quantitatively similar to *C. elegans* (Figure S2 in Additional file 2).

Ablating the ASH neurons in five nose-touch responsive species abolished nose-touch avoidance (Figure 5A). Four of the five species still responded in 20 to 30% of trials (Figure 5A). *Caenorhabditis* sp. 3 was the exception, as its ASH-ablated animals completely lost the ability to respond to nose touch (Figure 5A).

Ablation of the AWC neuron did not affect the response to nose touch in any of the species (Figure S3 in Additional file 2).

The alitrunk (Fig. 15) is conspicuously swollen and sits noticeably higher than the propodeal dorsum. The propodeum carries a pair of strong spines that are straight to slightly upcurved. The metanotal groove is absent, and the metapleural lobes are triangular and conspicuous. In profile, the petiole has an elongate peduncle and a well-developed node whose dorsum slopes downward posteriorly, leaving a short posterior face. On the postpetiole, the anterior and dorsal surfaces form a single convexity, and the posterior face is truncated. Seen from above, the nodes of both the petiole and the postpetiole are broader than long.

The dorsum of the head is strongly longitudinally rugose, with 5 to 7 rugae between the frontal carinae at eye-level. These rugae are irregular and meander slightly, and a few anastomoses are usually present. The scrobal area is largely smooth, though it typically carries 1–2 fine rugulae crossing its width just behind the antennal fossa. The sides of the head behind the eyes are finely reticulate-rugose, and this sculpture continues around the posterior margins of the scrobe to the occiput. The spaces between the rugae are unsculptured, or at most show faint superficial traces.

The dorsal alitrunk is everywhere finely but strongly reticulate-rugose, with broad, shining interspaces. The dorsum of the petiole is rugulose, while the postpetiole ranges from rugulose to only faintly sculptured. The gaster is unsculptured. All dorsal surfaces of the head and body are densely clothed with fine, acute hairs. The color ranges from dark reddish brown to blackish brown.

UPO-06: PrhI Gene Synthesis
UPO-06 contains the coding sequence for prhI from Ralstonia solanacearum, which encodes an ECF sigma factor needed for transcription driven by the Prh signal transduction system. PrhR activates the gene, which then directs sigma factor expression through activation of the PprhJ promoter. The sequence has been optimized for expression in Escherichia coli.

UPO-11: PprhJ Promoter Synthesis
UPO-11 provides the PprhJ promoter region, which responds to contact with plant cells through signal transduction mediated by PrhA and PrhR, and is activated by the ECF sigma factor PrhI. The sequence has been optimized for expression in Escherichia coli.

Subject: Key Findings on foxl2 Expression Patterns in Trout

Dear Customer,

Here is a summary of our findings on foxl2 transcript expression for your study.

Both foxl2 transcripts were expressed very early in development (Figure 2). foxl2a expression was highly restricted in the male, while the diverged paralog foxl2b was present in most adult extragonadal tissues examined (see Additional file 2).

In adult female tissues, foxl2b expression was limited to the skin, gill, and ovary. Expression in the testis was very strong, which agrees with earlier findings that foxl2b is present while foxl2a is absent in later stages of testis development in trout [23].

Taken together, these results suggest that foxl2b may act as a regulator of male-specific genes such as cyp19b1, particularly later in development.

Thank you for your interest in this work.

[10] Consequently, they do not have the attribute of additionality. Additionality asks the counterfactual question of what would have happened under the status quo if the REC had not been purchased or contracted. While there are many frameworks for testing additionality, the essential question is whether the project would have been financially viable without the sale of the RECs. Without evidence of additionality, RECs cannot be considered equivalent to emissions offsets.

A time-dependent mild-slope equation is derived following the formal derivation of Smith & Sprinks (1975), and from it we obtain the higher-order dispersion relation for waves over an uneven bottom. Using only the linear dispersion for steady waves, we recover equation (2.12) of Chamberlain & Porter (1995), known as the Modified Mild-Slope Equation (MMSE). The leading-order solution shows that the modified curvature terms of the MMSE have significant effects, while the slope square terms are negligible under the mild-slope assumption. Keeping all the modified curvature terms that are neglected in the MSE gives us a uniform model.

We then developed a numerical model based on the finite element method (FEM) to predict wave scattering by a varying bottom. In general, the uniform model predicts the salient features of waves over various sea beds, including sinusoidal beds and man-made bars. For sinusoidal beds, its results agree more closely with experimental data than those of other models. For man-made bars, both the MMSE and the uniform model agree more closely with the experimental data than the results of Kirby (1986).

The FEM model is also applied to the transformation of waves over an arbitrarily-varying bathymetry.

The myth of the Phaedrus is described with more intensity than any that came before it, though it belongs to a different sphere. It deals not with a future existence but with a former one, and it presents a struggle between reason, supported by passion or righteous indignation, and the animal instincts of our nature. In a former life the soul was in the company of some god and saw truth in the universal form before birth; our present life is the result of a previous struggle. Such a world is relative, and is often thrown forward into a future state, just as we speculate about where men were before they were born or what will become of them after death. The question "Where were men before birth?" is unfamiliar and unnatural to us, yet it is as real and as widely present as the other. In the Phaedrus the "spiritual combat" of this life is only a figure of speech, and the whole passage, especially the proem beginning "The mind through all her being is immortal," has a majesty and power that cannot be fully conveyed in another language.

When King's Cross station expanded north in the mid-1860s, its tracks cut through the grounds of St. Pancras Old Church, the oldest site of Christian worship in the city. Thomas Hardy, then working as an architect, was given the task of clearing the land. He exhumed the dead and arranged their gravestones in a spiral around a central tree. The tree is still there, but its roots have grown around the stones, and the inscriptions are becoming hard to read. Subject: A Note on the Legacy of Buraq

Dear Friend,

There was a time when the world made no firm distinction between reality and myth; that separation came only with modern comparative biology. Even so, science has never erased the liminal zone where a figure like Buraq lives. We need such transitional objects to connect empirical knowledge with spiritual experience.

In contemporary culture, her presence bridges rationalist taxonomies and the vestigial power of myth. Nowhere is this clearer than in the Islamic transport industry, where Buraq, a figure who combines piety and speed, recurs as a patron saint. Airlines from Libya to Indonesia carry her name, as do bus companies, freight ships, motorcycle taxis, a space camp, an engineering college, and Pakistan's first drone.

Part of what makes Buraq so pliable commercially is her fluidity as an aesthetic and linguistic object. She presides over wings and wheels, and she is also used to sell plastic and PVC, heavy metal, heavy-duty diesel (BURAQ LUBRICANTS), Indian food, and surgical instruments.

With appreciation for your curiosity,

Spider-Man: The Green Goblin's Trap

Videos showing a queue of dead bodies waiting for cremation outside a crematorium are being shared on social media. It is claimed that the bodies are of COVID-19 patients in Maharashtra. Human beings develop spoken language in the first few years of life. Hearing impairment can prevent the ability to speak and hinder the ability to understand spoken language. By the time it becomes apparent that a severely hearing-impaired (deaf) child has a hearing deficit, communication problems may already have caused issues within the family and hindered social skills. If the child is part of a Deaf community where sign language is used instead of spoken language, these challenges can be mitigated (please see our article on Deaf Culture).

In many developed countries, evaluations for hearing occur during the newborn period to prevent the inadvertent isolation of a deaf child within a hearing family. Although sign language is a full means of communication, literacy in the end depends on the ability to understand speech. In the vast majority of written language, the sound of the word is coded in symbols.

An individual who hears well enough to learn to speak and read will retain the ability to read even if their hearing becomes too impaired to hear voices. A person who never heard well enough to learn to speak is rarely able to read proficiently (see [4]). Most evidence suggests that the early identification of hearing impairment is key to ensuring a child with very insensitive hearing learns spoken language effectively. Listening also plays an important role in learning a second language.

Transduction is the process by which physical and chemical signals are converted into neural impulses. In the nervous system, it is the basic mechanism for translating stimuli into electrical signals. In sensory transduction, physical or chemical inputs are transformed by specialized sensory receptors into electrical impulses that travel to the brain.

The visual system offers a clear example. In the retina, rod and cone cells serve as the bridge between the physical environment and neural communication. When light strikes these photoreceptors, it triggers a conformational change in the protein rhodopsin. This molecular shift sets off a cascade of events that alters the electrochemical gradient of the photoreceptor. That reduction in the gradient causes a corresponding decrease in the electrical signals sent to the brain. In other words, more light hitting the photoreceptor produces fewer electrical impulses, which is how the brain decodes the visual world with such precision.

Mobile Gaming: The Next Evolution of Co-Creation

Mobile internet has expanded what electronic games can do for storytelling by putting them on portable, location-aware interfaces. This is the latest stage in a decades-long evolution of games that treat the player as more than an avatar in a gameworld, giving them a share of authorship alongside the original designers.

Location-aware interfaces let players fold real places into the gameworld and the gameworld back into real places, which no earlier interactive media had done. Mobile games also move away from linear narratives toward cooperative storytelling that depends on how the player experiences place.

The idea of "author-player" worldmaking is an old one, but mobile games push it past the limits of traditional video games. Because worldmaking extends beyond the screen into physical space, location-aware interfaces turn the player's sensory experience of real places into a storytelling tool.

In our essay, we theorize the unique storytelling potential of mobile games and describe our own attempt to realize that potential through the design and implementation of our hybrid-reality game, University of Death.

The Ruhr Area (German: Ruhrgebiet) is an urban region in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. It is made up of several former industrial cities: Duisburg, Oberhausen, Bottrop, Mülheim an der Ruhr, Essen, Gelsenkirchen, Bochum, Herne, Hamm, Hagen, Dortmund, Recklinghausen, Unna and Witten.

Around five million people live there, which makes the region considerably larger than Berlin, Hamburg or Munich. The motorway network is dense, yet hitchhiking can still be difficult because of the many minor roads. The main motorways are the A1, A2 and A3.

If you plan to hitchhike in the Ruhr Area, stay on these motorways. The smaller roads see very little transit traffic, which makes them a poor choice. Germany is generally a pleasant country for hitchhiking, but the Ruhr Area is the most difficult part of it. Hitching there is similar to hitching in a large city like Istanbul: the cities are independent, but to a traveler they all feel like districts of one huge city.
